A spate of companies have recently held back their updated artificial intelligence models over safety concerns. First, Anthropic withheld Mythos. Then, at the end of September, OpenAI scrapped the launch of GPT-6.1 Astra. The very next day, U.S. President Donald Trump gathered AI executives at the White House to sign a voluntary, “morally binding” accord to police themselves. The message? Any regulation stricter than self-policing risks China catching up on a thin U.S. lead.
But Matt Sheehan, co-director of the Carnegie Endowment’s China AI Initiative, points out that Beijing actually takes the opposite approach. It extensively regulates both AI development and deployment, and its companies are largely catching up with their American rivals anyway. Sheehan joins FP Live to discuss why the two AI superpowers govern the technology so differently and what the competition means for the future of geopolitics.

Host and Guests

Matt Sheehan

Co-director, Carnegie Endowment’s China AI Initiative

Matt Sheehan is a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, where he co-directs the China AI Initiative. Sheehan lived and worked in China from 2010 to 2016, and then was a fellow at the Paulson Institute’’s MacroPolo think tank, leading research on Chinese technology. He is the author of The Transpacific Experiment: How China and California Collaborate and Compete for Oour Future.

Can Development Work in Wartime?

October 2, 2026

How can you tackle poverty and create infrastructure amid an active conflict? Alexander De Croo is the head of the U.N. Development Program, and he joins FP’s Ravi Agrawal to make the case for spending development dollars on building long-term resilience. He’s exploring solutions to opium poppies in Afghanistan, electric grids in Ukraine, and sanitation in Gaza, even as major donors such as the United States pull back.

Mike Waltz on Trump’s Global Strategy

September 30, 2026

U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz has become one of the Trump administration’s most visible spokespeople, publicly explaining and defending its policies on everything from Iran to Venezuela and Sudan. How has Washington’s global role changed as the White House pulls back from multilateral institutions, including withdrawing from more than 30 U.N. entities and cutting the organization’s budget? Waltz joins FP Live for a wide-ranging conversation on U.S. foreign policy.

Maria Ressa on Fighting Back Against Big Tech

September 22, 2026

Maria Ressa is one of the most inspiring journalists of our age, a media leader whose bravery against authoritarianism earned her the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021. Now, she’s focusing her energy on artificial intelligence and Big Tech and how ordinary citizens can reclaim their attention, their time, and their democracies. Ressa joined Ravi Agrawal on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly this week at FP’s Tech and AI Forum.

How to Create A Billion Jobs

September 21, 2026

Ajay Banga has a simple north star as he runs the World Bank: jobs, jobs, jobs. And for good reason. The World Bank estimates developing countries are on track to create only a third of the approximately 1.2 billion jobs they will need to keep up with demand. How can countries and companies bridge this gap? Banga sat down with FP’s Ravi Agrawal to detail how the bank is mobilizing private capital to launch a massive infrastructure drive in the developing world and create sustainable jobs.
